title: MDCAT Biology: Highest-Weightage Chapters
excerpt: Biology carries the biggest share of the MDCAT paper — here's which chapters test-prep analysis consistently flags as high-yield, and how to use that to order your revision.

content.text: Why "highest-weightage" doesn't mean the same thing everywhere

If you've searched around, you've probably already noticed that different sources give different exact numbers for how MDCAT marks are split — some cite one total question count, others cite another, and per-chapter weightage figures vary depending on which years of past papers were analyzed. None of these blogs, including this one, are the syllabus itself.

Don't memorize a specific mark count per chapter from any blog, including this one. Use the official PMDC Uniform Curriculum for the topic list, and use past papers (not secondhand percentage claims) to judge how often a chapter's content actually shows up.

What test-prep analysis does agree on, fairly consistently, is which chapters tend to come up often across past MDCAT papers — even when the exact percentage attached to each one differs by source. That consistency is more useful to you than any single number, so that's what this post focuses on.
The chapters that show up again and again
Across multiple years of past-paper analysis, a handful of Biology areas are named repeatedly as high-yield:

items: Human Physiology — support and movement, circulation, respiration, and reproduction
Coordination and control (nervous and endocrine systems)

content.text: If you've already built a rough revision order for Biology, checking it against this list is a reasonable sanity check — not because any one blog has the "real" weightage, but because these are the areas that consistently reappear when people actually count MCQs from real past papers.
Why Human Physiology deserves special attention

Of everything on that list, Human Physiology tends to get singled out most often — it spans several FSc chapters (circulation, respiration, excretion, nervous coordination, reproduction), and MDCAT questions frequently connect concepts across these systems rather than testing one chapter in isolation. A question might ask you to link a hormone's effect on the kidneys with its effect on blood pressure, for instance — which means memorizing each chapter separately isn't enough. You need to be able to move between them.

This is also the section where FSc-level familiarity can be misleading. You may have done well on a Physiology unit test that focused on one chapter at a time — MDCAT physiology questions often don't respect those chapter boundaries.
Genetics: fewer chapters, disproportionate return

Genetics is a relatively compact part of the Biology syllabus compared to something like Diversity of Life, but it consistently punches above its size in terms of how often it's tested. It also tends to be one of the more logic-based parts of Biology — once you understand the underlying principles (inheritance patterns, pedigree analysis, molecular genetics basics), the questions become more about applying logic than pure memorization, which makes it one of the more efficient chapters to master relative to time invested.
Diversity of Life: broad, but pattern-heavy

Diversity of Life covers a lot of ground — classification, kingdoms, and characteristics across different groups of organisms — and it can feel like pure memorization at first glance. In practice, MDCAT tends to test comparisons (how one group differs from another) more than isolated facts about a single organism. Building comparison tables as you study, rather than reading each group in isolation, tends to make this section faster to revise closer to the exam.
Cell Biology and Biological Molecules: your foundation, not an afterthought

These two chapters come early in the FSc syllabus, which sometimes means they get treated as "already done" by the time MDCAT prep starts in earnest. That's a mistake — cell structure and biomolecules (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids) underpin a lot of later physiology and genetics content, and MDCAT papers do return to them directly, not just as background knowledge for other chapters.
Turning this into a revision order
A reasonable way to sequence Biology revision, based on the pattern above, is:

items: Start with Cell Biology and Biological Molecules, since they support everything after
Move into Genetics, since it's compact and logic-driven once the fundamentals click
Spend the most sustained time on Human Physiology, given both its breadth and how often it's tested
Treat Diversity of Life as a comparison-building exercise rather than isolated memorization
Circle back to lower-frequency chapters last, once the high-yield areas are solid

content.text: If you want to check your own weak areas against this order, working through timed chapter-wise MCQs — rather than only rereading notes — will tell you more about where you actually stand than any weightage percentage will.

Always verify the current chapter list and topic depth against the official PMDC MDCAT syllabus before finalizing your study plan — chapter emphasis can shift slightly between test cycles, and this post reflects patterns from past papers, not a guaranteed blueprint for the next one.
The bottom line

You won't find one universally agreed-upon percentage for each Biology chapter, and you shouldn't trust any source — including this one — that states one with total confidence. What's more reliable is the recurring pattern: Human Physiology, Genetics, Coordination and Control, and Diversity of Life show up consistently across past papers, and Cell Biology and Biological Molecules quietly support all of them. Build your revision order around that pattern, verify it against real past papers as you go, and keep the official syllabus as your ground truth.

items.question: Which MDCAT Biology chapters carry the most weight?
items.answer: Human Physiology, Genetics and inheritance, Coordination and Control, Diversity of Life, and Cell Biology/Biological Molecules consistently appear as high-yield across past-paper analysis, even though exact percentage figures vary by source.

items.question: Is there an official percentage weightage for each Biology chapter?
items.answer: No single, universally agreed figure exists across sources for chapter-level weightage. Use the official PMDC Uniform Curriculum for the topic list, and past papers rather than secondhand percentage claims to judge how often a chapter's content actually appears.

items.question: Why does Human Physiology need extra attention specifically?
items.answer: It spans several FSc chapters (circulation, respiration, excretion, nervous coordination, reproduction), and MDCAT questions frequently connect concepts across these systems rather than testing one chapter in isolation — memorizing each chapter separately isn't enough.

items.question: What order should I revise MDCAT Biology chapters in?
items.answer: A reasonable sequence: start with Cell Biology and Biological Molecules (they support everything else), move into Genetics (compact and logic-driven), spend the most time on Human Physiology, treat Diversity of Life as a comparison-building exercise, then circle back to lower-frequency chapters last.

items.question: Is Genetics worth prioritizing even though it's a smaller topic?
items.answer: Yes — Genetics is compact relative to a topic like Diversity of Life but consistently punches above its size in how often it's tested, and it's more logic-based than memorization-heavy once the underlying principles click, making it efficient to master.
